name: Yusuf Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to employers, political parties or AI firms. Your answers stay confidential. Yusuf, what does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the permit, count the fittings in the van and then spend the day repairing overhead lines with our crew. I like teaching a younger worker why a joint fails, not just how to tighten it. Wrong stock counts and a late drive back to the depot wear me down, especially when I miss supper with the children.

say: I would welcome **faster fault entry** if field safety checks stay with the crew.
I would say **line repairs** still need people on the pole.
think: I use **AI occasionally** for manual searches after other crews have tested them.
Our **thin savings** and mortgage make missed shifts a household problem.
do: Keep paid **repair shifts** and verify AI results against paper manuals.
Put one weekly **café cost** into a car repair jar from next wage.
feel: I feel **comfortable at work** and uneasy about irregular school and car costs.
S0.quote: A quick search is useful only when the safety instruction is the one we actually use.
fieldNote: Yusuf adopts a **tested manual search** but checks the printed safety page and asks his lead about it.
A recent **clutch repair** paid in instalments shows why minor AI change leaves household anxiety intact.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and verify manual searches against printed pages
Put one weekly café cost into a car repair jar

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that the tablet can fill in a fault number if it saves a few minutes. Somebody still has to climb, check the isolation and replace the damaged fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then to find the right page in a manual, after another crew has tried the search. My bigger worry is the mortgage, because our savings would not cover a month if the van failed and I missed shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid repair rota and check any AI result against the paper manual. Starting with the next wage, my partner and I would put the cost of one weekly café stop into a jar for car repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable with the line work and uneasy with our budget. The children need school things at odd times, and a small delay in wages sends us to the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What made you think about car repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The clutch started slipping in October and we paid the mechanic in two instalments. I would rather see a little money waiting before the next visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a manual search trustworthy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask the lead which section to check and compare the page number with the printed copy. A quick search is useful only when the safety instruction is the one we actually use.

say: I would ask for **ten accurate jobs** before rolling out the ordering tablet.
I would keep a **physical fitting check** in apprentice training.
think: The **stores staff** may shrink first, leaving field crews to catch costly order errors.
I want proof the tablet helps before giving up **reliable clerk checks**.
do: Stay on paid **line work** and shadow the first tablet crew for a shift.
Compare **tablet orders** with actual fittings in the first rollout year.
feel: I feel **cautious and curious** about a tool tested by colleagues.
S1.quote: I would not trade a reliable clerk for a pretty screen without proof.
fieldNote: Yusuf waits for a **colleague-tested tool** and defines a practical ten-job threshold before using it himself.
His **apprenticeship memory** makes physical fittings central to teaching and to evaluating automated orders.

steps.text: Continue paid line work while the first crew tests tablet orders
Shadow the first crew on paid time and compare AI orders with fittings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stores team to try a computer order if it brings the right gear to our van. I would ask the first crew to test it for a few weeks before the whole depot changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and buying jobs could shrink at the depot before robots touch our field work. If fewer people catch order mistakes, we may lose an afternoon of paid repairs to driving back for a part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on line work and ask to shadow the first crew using the new ordering tablet for one paid shift. In its first year I would compare the tablet order with the fittings we use and tell the supervisor when a repeated error costs time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious and curious. A tool that gets the right gear could help us finish before school pickup, but I would not trade a reliable clerk for a pretty screen without proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you say the trial worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the first crew can complete ten jobs without a second trip for missing parts, I would try it. I would also ask the stores clerk whether the stock count matched what the tablet showed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your apprenticeship matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My first supervisor made me touch and name every fitting before I used a drawing. I would show a younger worker the physical part before asking them to trust its name on a tablet.

say: I would separate **2028 work orders** from field robots around 2031.
I would ask for a **human crew** beside early robot repairs.
think: I will be **48** when robots arrive, with children and a mortgage.
Our **small cushion** could not carry a long gap in wages.
do: Keep paid **callouts** after 2028 and ask about field-checking vacancies.
Cut **hotel spending** on family visits and take paid training if tied to a posted job.
feel: I feel **frightened by speed** but expect paid line work for the three-year gap.
S2.quote: The three years before line-repair robots arrive could give me time to find a real paid opening.
fieldNote: Yusuf treats the **three-year robot lag** as time for paid line work and a search for field-checking posts.
He cuts a specific **family hotel cost** but keeps visiting relatives, matching his priority on family ties.

steps.text: Keep paid line callouts in the first 2028 AI year
Apply for a posted paid field-checking vacancy if available
Skip the hotel on family visits to reserve mortgage cash
Take company-paid hands-on robot training if tied to a posted job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 could write our orders, but robots that can repair lines come closer to 2031. I would want the company to keep a human crew beside early robot jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 at the first date and 48 when robots arrive. Our two children would still need us, and the mortgage plus less than a month of savings makes even a short wage gap serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager whether the company will pay experienced lineworkers to check robot repairs. In the first year after 2028 I would keep the callouts, apply for a paid field-checking vacancy if one is posted and reduce our family travel spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel frightened by the speed, but I do not expect my line shifts to end in 2028. The three years before line-repair robots arrive could give me time to find a real paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What travel would you change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We usually take the children to my parents for a long weekend and stay at a small hotel. We could visit for a day and keep the hotel money for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a robot course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a company-paid hands-on course if it qualified me for a posted field-checking job. I would not pay for lessons on my own when there are so few similar jobs nearby.

say: I would ask for a **connector trial** on an awkward span.
I would distinguish **2031 office AI** from hands-on robots around 2034.
think: At **51**, I may still need a full wage and cannot assume retirement.
A **report-heavy role** may shrink once full AI handles the writing.
do: Keep the paid **field rota** and request a supervised robot demonstration.
In **2031**, take paid inspection training if tied to a posted field role.
feel: I feel **less rushed** with time to see real trials.
S3.quote: A person should inspect the finished joint before anyone calls the trial a success.
fieldNote: Yusuf wants **hands-on proof** on an awkward span and remains skeptical of a smooth training-pad display.
His concern for an **apprentice path** extends to his child, yet he does not promise the old field career will persist.

steps.text: Continue paid field repairs through the first 2031 AI year
Take company-paid field inspection training if tied to an opening
Apply for a field inspection job once pay and duties are written

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough to see a robot repair a line with the crew watching. Full thinking AI arrives in 2031, and hands-on robots around 2034, so an office plan and a field repair are different dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the office changes and 51 at the robot date. The older child may be finishing school, but the mortgage may still be there and I cannot assume retirement at 51.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a paid demonstration at the depot and keep my field rota. In 2031 I would stay on paid repairs, take a company-paid field inspection course if it leads to an opening and apply only when its wage and duties are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed because the children would be older and I would have time to look at real trial results. I would still be careful about a job that is mainly writing reports, since full AI could take that work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the demonstration have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the robot to fit a connector on an awkward span, not just pick up tools on level ground. A person should inspect the finished joint before anyone calls the trial a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you encourage your child to enter the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my older child the apprenticeship teaches useful hands-on skill, but the company must explain what the field jobs look like after robots. I cannot promise the old path will stay the same.

say: I would call for **real job trials** before changing line crew numbers.
I would separate **2036 planning AI** from physical robots around 2039.
think: At **56**, I cannot assume grown children erase mortgage costs or fund retirement.
A **field inspection role** needs regular pay after AI takes planning work.
do: Keep paid **line repairs** and pay extra mortgage principal from dependable standby.
In **2036**, compare field hours and apply for a posted inspection role if pay holds.
feel: I feel **steady now** and cautious about retirement claims.
S4.quote: I would not tell a young person to rely on a pension that nobody has promised.
fieldNote: Yusuf expects **continued paid line work** over the near term and asks for tested, posted field roles before changing jobs.
His **family budget** limits mortgage overpayments to months with dependable standby income.

steps.text: Continue paid line repair shifts through the first 2036 AI year
Pay thirty extra mortgage principal in months with two standby shifts
Apply for a posted field inspection role if pay and duties hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot a decade is long enough to test machines on the jobs we actually do. Full AI in 2036 changes planning first; robots that can work the lines come around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 for the planning change and 56 when robots arrive. Our children may have grown up, but I cannot count on an empty house paying the mortgage or providing a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stay on line repairs and put a little from dependable standby pay toward mortgage principal. In 2036 I would compare field hours with my partner, keep working the line while needed and apply for a posted inspection role if its field duties and wage held up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the next few years. The longer warning gives me time to keep earning and judge a real opening, though I would not set a retirement date by the robot timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you add to the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a month with two standby shifts I could add thirty to the usual payment. In a month without them, the children and bills come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still teach apprentices in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach a new apprentice to inspect a connector by hand and to ask the company which field roles are funded. I would not tell a young person to rely on a pension that nobody has promised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the three years before field robots arrive are short for a family with almost no savings. Paid hands-on training linked to a posted inspection role and clear robot trial results would help me keep earning while I decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to apprentices if a machine takes the routine repairs. The company should show a young worker a real path to paid field skill before recruiting them.

headlineQuote: The company should show a young worker a real path to paid field skill before recruiting them.
portrait: Yusuf is a **43-year-old lineworker** with an apprenticeship, a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** for manual searches after other crews have tested the tool.
His **thin savings** and recent car repair make steady paid shifts essential.
Across the scenarios he seeks **hands-on trials**, posted field roles and paid training that protects family income.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** gives his household only about three years before capable robots reach field repairs.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **hands-on training**, a posted inspection job and clear robot trial results would help him keep earning.
